extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics and computer science students learning to read and write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for constructing and checking correct, clear mathematical proofs (proof strategies, use of logic, quantifier handling, induction, and use of the Proof Designer tool). Aimed at teaching structured proving and common inference techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose proof structure guided by logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of proof structure is guided by the logical form of the statement being proven (e.g., use suppose-until for 'if P then Q', use 'for arbitrary x prove' for universal statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the logical form of the theorem first and then select basic proof structures (suppose-until, for arbitrary x prove, existence witness, induction, proof by contradiction, proof by cases) and combine/nest them as appropriate; use indenting or structure internally while aiming to write in ordinary English paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'suppose-until' for conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement of the form 'if P then Q', suppose P is true until you reach Q, then discharge the supposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'suppose-until' structure can be nested inside other structures (e.g., inside 'let x be arbitrary' for universal conditionals). In Proof Designer: select the goal and give the Direct command in the Strategy menu. Alternatively prove the contrapositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'for arbitrary x prove' for universals
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a universal statement 'for all x, P(x)', declare x to be an arbitrary object and prove P(x); then retract and conclude the universal statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a letter is already in use, pick a different variable name. In Proof Designer: select the goal and give the Arbitrary Object command in the Strategy menu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write proofs in ordinary English paragraphs but understand nested structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Although underlying proof structure can be displayed with indenting, aim to write proofs in ordinary English paragraphs like mathematicians do, while ensuring the structural moves (e.g., 'Let x be arbitrary', 'Suppose P') are used appropriately to introduce proof structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using structural phrases inappropriately (analogous to using 'do' without a matching 'while' in programming). Indenting is a teaching device; final writing should be fluent English reflecting the structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexpress a negated goal positively or use contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form ¬P: (a) reexpress as a positive statement; (b) use proof by contradiction (assume P and derive a contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer: select the goal, give the Reexpress command and use Reexpress Negative, or give the Contradiction command in the Strategy menu (optionally select the given you plan to contradict).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove implications by direct proof or contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal P → Q: (a) assume P and prove Q (direct); (b) prove the contrapositive: assume ¬Q and prove ¬P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Proof Designer: select the goal and give the Direct command, or give the Contrapositive command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove conjunctions by proving each conjunct
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal P ∧ Q, prove P and prove Q separately (treat as two goals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one conjunct is already known as a given, select it and use the Conjunction or Split Up commands in the Infer menu in Proof Designer so you only have to prove the remaining conjunct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove disjunctions by assuming negation or using cases
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal P ∨ Q: (a) assume ¬P and prove Q, or assume ¬Q and prove P; (b) use proof by cases (split into exhaustive cases and prove P ∨ Q in each).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer: select the goal and give the Disjunction command (it will ask which statement you plan to prove), or use the Cases command in the Strategy menu and then Disjunction in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove biconditionals by proving both directions
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P ↔ Q, prove P → Q and Q → P using the methods listed for implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Proof Designer: select the goal and give the Biconditional command in the Strategy menu (it will guide you to prove both directions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove existential goals by giving a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃x P(x), find and present a specific value w such that P(w) holds, and prove P(w).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the witness is not obvious, introduce a variable to stand for the intended value and fill it in later. Proof Designer: select the goal and give the Existence command; it will ask what value to use for x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove uniqueness-existence goals by two-part proof or reexpression
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃!x P(x): (a) prove existence and then prove uniqueness (∀y∀z((P(y) ∧ P(z)) → y = z)); (b) prove an equivalent reexpressed form  ∃x(P(x) ∧ ∀y(P(y) → y = x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer: use the Existence & Uniqueness command or use Reexpress and Apply Definition to transform the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove universal numeric statements by induction or strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∀n ∈ N P(n): (a) standard induction: prove base case P(0) and inductive step ∀n(P(n) → P(n+1)); (b) strong induction: prove ∀n[(∀k < n P(k)) → P(n)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate base cases and clearly state the inductive hypothesis; Proof Designer includes commands to structure induction steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens with conditional givens
rubrics_metrics.description: Given P → Q: (a) if P is also given or can be proved, conclude Q (Modus Ponens); (b) if ¬Q is given or provable, conclude ¬P (Modus Tollens/contrapositive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer: select the givens P and P → Q and give Modus Ponens in the Infer menu; or select ¬Q and P → Q and give Modus Tollens to infer ¬P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split conjunctive givens
rubrics_metrics.description: Given P ∧ Q, treat it as two givens P and Q (split it up to use either conjunct independently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer: select the given and give the Split Up command in the Infer menu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disjunctive givens by cases or disjunctive syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: Given P ∨ Q: (a) apply proof by cases to use the disjunction productively; (b) if ¬P (or ¬Q) is known, conclude Q (or P) by disjunctive syllogism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer: select the given and give the Cases command in the Strategy menu, or select −P (or −Q) and P ∨ Q and give Disjunctive Syllogism in the Infer menu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat biconditional givens as two conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Given P ↔ Q, treat it as two givens P → Q and Q → P for inference purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer: select the biconditional given and give the Split Up command in the Infer menu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use universal givens by instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ∀x P(x), you may instantiate (plug in) any specific value a to conclude P(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure what to plug in, introduce a variable placeholder and decide later. Proof Designer: select the given and give Universal Instantiation in the Infer menu; it will ask what to plug in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existential givens by instantiation/introduction of witness variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ∃x P(x), introduce a new variable x0 that stands for a particular object for which P(x0) is true (existential instantiation); you may also assume the uniqueness condition if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Proof Designer: select the given and give the Existential Instantiation command and follow the prompts; for unique-existential you may also assume ∀y(P(y) → y = x0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction as a general technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the goal and derive a contradiction with the givens or derived statements; then conclude the original goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widely applicable; in Proof Designer select the goal and give the Contradiction command. If you already know which given you will contradict, select it too to focus the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases as a general technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the proof into exhaustive cases covering all possibilities and prove the goal in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Proof Designer, selecting a disjunction given and giving the Cases command will create case subproofs; you can also supply a distinguishing predicate as a case split for a goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured presentation and management of subproofs/gaps (Proof Designer workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can be viewed as a sequence of steps, subproofs, and gaps; each gap has givens and a goal. Use subproofs to justify steps and variants for equivalent forms; hide/show subproof detail to manage complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer specifics: click givens/goals to select, use menus to add steps, subproofs are indented and boxed (with a '.:.' button), variants are shown indented under originals, drag to reorder givens, hide details with '.' or '?' buttons, and export via Export HTML.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use truth tables and connective semantics to judge validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how logical connectives (and, or, not, implication, biconditional) affect truth values using truth tables to determine validity of arguments and to understand main connective and scope/parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mathematics 'or' is inclusive unless specified; use truth tables to settle ambiguous English phrasing. Be careful with parentheses and conventions (− applies only to immediately following statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain well-formed logical formulas and watch for hidden logical structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Only certain symbol strings are grammatical as formulas (well-formed formulas). Also expand mathematical notation (e.g., chained inequalities) to reveal hidden logical connectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check grammar of formulas (avoid meaningless strings). When seeing expressions like 3 < a < 4, expand to logical form ( (3 < a ∨ 3 = a) ∧ (a < 4) ) to clarify reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When stuck, reexpress givens/goals or use variant forms
rubrics_metrics.description: You may reexpress a negative statement as a positive equivalent or generate variant equivalent forms of given/goal statements to make applicable rules more apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof Designer: use Reexpress command (Reexpress Negative, Apply Definition) to produce variants that can be selected and used like the originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply common inference rules explicitly (modus ponens, modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism, universal/existential rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and apply standard rules of inference: Modus Ponens (from P and P→Q infer Q), Modus Tollens (from ¬Q and P→Q infer ¬P), Disjunctive Syllogism (from P∨Q and ¬P infer Q), Universal Instantiation, Existential Instantiation, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as mechanical steps when appropriate; Proof Designer contains menu commands to perform these inferences and will request the necessary selections (givens/targets).
